blockMcqs.question: What defines a domain-specific architecture?
options: A chip that runs any workload equally well
A chip built to do one job extremely well
A CPU with a faster clock speed
Any chip made after 2010
blockMcqs.explanation: A DSA trades general flexibility for high efficiency at one specific task.

blockMcqs.question: What did the end of Dennard scaling cause?
options: Transistors got cheaper to shrink forever
Clock speeds kept rising for free
Smaller transistors began leaking more power
Moore's Law sped up
blockMcqs.explanation: Once shrinking transistors stopped cutting power per transistor, clock speed gains for free ended.

blockMcqs.question: Why build hardware around one workload?
options: It's cheaper to manufacture than any CPU
General CPU speed gains have slowed
It requires no design effort
It runs every task equally fast
blockMcqs.explanation: With general-purpose speedups stalling, efficiency gains now come from specializing hardware.

blockMcqs.question: What do you give up moving from CPU to ASIC?
options: Power efficiency
Peak throughput on the target task
Flexibility to run other tasks
Manufacturing cost stays the same
blockMcqs.explanation: ASICs gain efficiency on one job but lose the ability to run anything else.

blockMcqs.question: What is a key downside of an ASIC?
options: It cannot be manufactured at scale
Its logic can't change after fabrication
It always uses more power than a CPU
It can only run one instruction set
blockMcqs.explanation: ASIC circuits are fixed at manufacturing, so mistakes or new needs require a whole new chip.

blockMcqs.question: What makes an FPGA different from an ASIC?
options: It has no logic circuits at all
It can be rewired after manufacturing
It is always faster than an ASIC
It only runs machine learning code
blockMcqs.explanation: FPGAs use reconfigurable logic blocks, so the circuit can change after the chip is made.

blockMcqs.question: What operation do DSPs repeat constantly?
options: Branch prediction
Multiply-then-add on data streams
Disk file lookups
Instruction decoding
blockMcqs.explanation: DSPs are built around fast, repeated multiply-accumulate operations on streaming signal data.

blockMcqs.question: What core operation are TPUs/NPUs built for?
options: Matrix multiplication for neural networks
General-purpose branch handling
Video file compression only
Disk I/O scheduling
blockMcqs.explanation: TPUs and NPUs are ASICs specialized for the matrix math neural networks repeat heavily.

blockMcqs.question: Why does RISC-V matter for building DSAs?
options: It is a closed, licensed instruction set
It is open and extensible with custom instructions
It only works inside Google's TPUs
It replaces the need for any ISA
blockMcqs.explanation: RISC-V's open, extensible design lets teams add domain-specific instructions cheaply.

blockMcqs.question: What is a chiplet-based design?
options: One giant die with no specialization
Small separate dies combined in one package
A single-core CPU only
A chip with no I/O support
blockMcqs.explanation: Chiplets combine multiple smaller dies in one package instead of one giant monolithic die.

blockMcqs.question: Which statement about specialization is correct?
options: CPUs are becoming fully obsolete
FPGAs are just slower, cheaper ASICs
A chip is only faster on its intended workload
Specialized hardware never wastes energy anywhere
blockMcqs.explanation: Specialized hardware wins only on the workload it was built for, not universally.
